Article Title: King Charles sold a young racehorse to Australian owners just months before it won the Melbourne Cup on only its sixth career start; the horse led its new trainer to an unprecedented sweep of the top
Article Text:
Jockey Ethan Brown reacts as he rides Point Of Law to win the Melbourne Cup horse race in Melbourne, Australia, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

A royal sale that became a headline

Britain's King Charles REUTERS/Isabel Infantes/Pool

A race built for a stayer

Jockey Ethan Brown reacts on Point Of Law after winning the Melbourne Cup horse race in Melbourne, Australia, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

Maher’s unprecedented trifecta

Brown’s moment to remember

Jockey Ethan Brown celebrates with his partner Celine Gaudray after riding Point Of Law to win the Melbourne Cup horse race in Melbourne, Australia, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

A new chapter for Point of Law

Racing rarely brings out stories this amusing. A young colt once owned by King Charles III was sold to Australian interests, placed in Ciaron Maher’s stable, and then produced the performance of his short career in the race Australia stops for. The horse named Point of Law won the Melbourne Cup at Flemington on November 3, 2026, in only his sixth career start, having never previously raced over the demanding 3,200 metre distance, according to AFP.The victory carried an extra twist. Maher did not merely train the winner. His horses finished first, second and third, with Point of Law leading home stablemates Zahrann and Juja Kibo. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported that this was the first time in the Melbourne Cup’s 166 editions that one trainer had filled the entire top three.For Maher, it was a second Melbourne Cup triumph, but the scale of this result was entirely different. For Ethan Brown, the jockey who rode Point of Law, it was a first success in Australia’s most famous race. And for the horse’s former royal owners, it was the kind of result that turns a routine sale into an unforgettable piece of racing folklore. Read more about this unexpected twist-of-fate story, as per ABC and AFP reports, here:Point of Law began his racing life in Britain, where he was previously owned by King Charles and Queen Camilla.He was then purchased by Maher, making Australia his new racing home and setting up the remarkable sequence that followed. AFP described the purchase as Maher’s acquisition from King Charles, with the Melbourne Cup representing the colt’s Australian debut. That detail gives the result its human appeal. Racing owners sell horses for many practical reasons, from stable planning to bloodstock strategy, and few could have predicted that this particular three-year-old would become the central figure in a Melbourne Cup for the ages. The sale did not simply change Point of Law’s address. It placed him with a trainer capable of preparing him for one of the toughest staying tests in world racing.By the time he reached Flemington, Point of Law had already signalled that something special might be coming. He won the Geelong Cup in his Australian debut, a lead-up performance that excited bookmakers and gave Maher confidence that the horse could handle the step up in distance. AFP noted that he entered the Melbourne Cup as a short-priced favourite after that powerful Geelong display.The Melbourne Cup is not a sprint disguised as a marathon. Run over 3,200 metres, it tests stamina, patience, balance and nerve. It has been contested since 1861 and remains such a major part of Victorian life that race day is a public holiday in the state. This year’s renewal developed in unusually dramatic fashion. Royal Supremacy, another Maher runner, broke from barrier 21 and went forward early. By the 1,500 metre mark, he had opened an eight-length lead over the 23-horse field. With 1,000 metres remaining, that advantage had stretched to 20 lengths, creating the kind of front-running spectacle that can either become a famous steal or collapse into a cautionary tale.Royal Supremacy kept finding more for longer than most expected. He still held a commanding 12-length lead at the 400 metre mark, according to the ABC. But the final Flemington straight is long, and the pace eventually began to tell. Point of Law, ridden patiently by Brown, emerged from behind the leaders and swept past with about 150 metres to run.The winning margin was 3.75 lengths. It was not a narrow scramble, but a decisive change of momentum in the closing stages, with the favourite showing the acceleration that separates a good stayer from a genuine Cup winner.Maher had seven runners in the race, an extraordinary commitment in itself. Yet even he could not have scripted the outcome. Point of Law won, Zahrann finished second and Juja Kibo took third, giving the stable the first trainer-led trifecta in Melbourne Cup history.“This is what the Melbourne Cup is all about,” Maher said after the race, according to the ABC. He described Point of Law as a horse that had thrived and thanked his team and owners for their work throughout the campaign. He also called the achievement of having three horses fill the top three positions remarkable.The result was especially striking because Maher’s other runners did not simply disappear. Royal Supremacy, after his bold front-running effort, finished fifth. Shockletz was sixth. Only Mr Monaco failed to make an impact, coming home 17th. That depth of performance underlined that this was not a lucky result for one horse but an exceptionally strong training performance across an entire team.For Brown, the win carried a personal weight beyond the trophy. It was his first Melbourne Cup victory, and he rode the race with the calm assurance of someone who understood that the early leader might not be the horse to follow. His decision to wait, then deliver Point of Law at the right time, proved decisive.Afterwards, Brown struggled to put the experience into words. “Don’t wake me up. Amazing feeling,” he told AFP. He also praised Maher for standing by him through earlier mistakes and continuing to give him opportunities on important horses.The ABC reported that Brown reflected on Maher’s support since he was around 22 years old, saying the trainer had believed in him despite errors on his horses. When Brown collected the trophy, he admitted he had to pinch himself. It was a reminder that, for all the money, history and spectacle surrounding the Melbourne Cup, the sport still turns on individual relationships between trainers, jockeys and horses.Point of Law’s story now has an almost improbable shape. A three-year-old formerly owned by Britain’s King is sold to Australia, joins one of the country’s leading stables, wins a major lead-up race, then captures the Melbourne Cup at his sixth career start. AFP emphasised that he had never raced beyond 3,200 metres before Flemington, making the performance even more impressive.The horse’s next chapters will be watched closely. Winners of the Melbourne Cup instantly become part of Australian racing history, and Point of Law has already earned a place among the race’s most memorable champions. But whatever comes next, Tuesday’s result will be remembered for more than the trophy.It will be remembered as the day a former royal racehorse repaid his new connections in the most public way possible, while helping his trainer achieve something no one had managed in 166 runnings of the race. As Maher put it, it has been a whirlwind. For Australian racing, it was also a day that showed why the Melbourne Cup continues to capture imaginations far beyond the track.
Article Summary: Point of Law won the Melbourne Cup at Flemington on November 3, 2026, in only his sixth career start. The horse had never previously raced over the demanding 3,200 metre distance. Point of Law began his racing life in Britain, where he was previously owned by King Charles and Queen Camilla. He was then purchased by Maher, making Australia his new racing home.

Article Title: ‘Habibi, call me Senator’: First Muslim US Senator Abdul El-Sayed mocks Donald Trump, JD Vance in victory speech
Article Text:
Abdul El-Sayed trolls Trump, JD Vance after winning Michigan Senate race

El-Sayed's campaign and attacks from Trump

Democratic gains reshape Senate politics

Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Wednesday took a swipe at US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race, using his victory speech to highlight the irony of Vance having to formally swear him into office.Addressing Vance, El-Sayed said, “Habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in, in January.”He also directed a pointed message at Trump, who had repeatedly criticised him during the campaign and questioned his loyalty to the United States.“I know you struggle with my name, so after JD swears me in, you can just go on and call me Senator,” El-Sayed said.El-Sayed's victory makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. He defeated Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who had Trump's backing, in a closely watched contest for Michigan's open Senate seat.El-Sayed also took aim at Rogers during his victory speech, telling supporters, “You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope.”The son of Egyptian immigrants, El-Sayed is a former public health official who had never held elected office before winning the Senate race. His victory followed a difficult political journey, eight years after he suffered a double-digit defeat in Michigan's Democratic gubernatorial primary.His campaign was built around a progressive platform that included universal healthcare, removing outside money from elections and criticism of Israel. He received support from progressive leaders, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.The campaign was marked by repeated attacks from Trump and other Republicans, who sought to link El-Sayed to terrorist organisations despite no evidence of such ties. They also questioned his loyalty to the US.El-Sayed's criticism of Israel became a major point of contention, including during a bruising Democratic primary against Representative Haley Stevens. The primary drew nearly $60 million in outside spending, with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spending nearly $30 million opposing him, its largest investment in a single race.Stevens, who lost the primary, endorsed Rogers on November 1, saying El-Sayed had not done enough to address her and the Jewish community's concerns.El-Sayed also faced criticism over remarks following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologised, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful”.El-Sayed's win came as Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, according to Reuters. His victory was among several gains for the party in states that have traditionally favoured Republicans.The Michigan contest became a major focus in the battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Senator Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election.Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Representative Elissa Slotkin in 2024.However, his campaign faced challenges over his support for Trump as voters expressed concerns about rising prices linked to the war with Iran and the economic impact of the president's tariffs.Rogers, who had previously criticised Trump, had aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years.He had also voiced concern about the war with Iran, writing on social media in September, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”El-Sayed's victory is expected to strengthen the progressive wing of the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential election.His campaign demonstrated the electoral reach of a platform centred on policies such as Medicare for All, which would replace the existing mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system.
Article Summary: Abdul El-Sayed is the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. He defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a closely watched contest for Michigan's open Senate seat. His victory is expected to strengthen the progressive wing of the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Article Title: Drag queen who raised $3.7 million for environmental causes sued by outdoor giant Patagonia over her name, Pattie Gonia; company seeks just $1 in damages
Article Text:
Pattie Gonia, the drag persona of environmental activist Wyn Wiley, poses at an event. Image: pattiegonia/Instagram

Who is Pattie Gonia and how did she become an environmental activist?

Why is Patagonia suing Pattie Gonia?

Why is Patagonia seeking just $1 in damages?

Pattie Gonia says the lawsuit threatens her identity and work

Trademark dispute reaches the US trademark board

A drag performer who has raised $3.7 million for environmental causes is locked in a legal battle with one of the world's best-known outdoor clothing companies over a name that has become central to her activism. Pattie Gonia, the stage persona of environmental activist Wyn Wiley, is being sued by Patagonia over alleged trademark infringement. The California-based outdoor apparel company filed the lawsuit in January 2026, claiming that the name, merchandise and designs associated with the performer could create confusion with its established brand. The unusual part of the case is the amount Patagonia is seeking, just $1 in monetary damages. However, the dispute goes beyond money, with the company also seeking restrictions on the use of the name.Pattie Gonia is the drag persona created by environmental activist and performer Wyn Wiley, who identifies as non-binary. Wiley uses they/them pronouns out of drag, while Pattie Gonia uses she/her pronouns as a drag character. The persona first attracted attention in 2018 after Wiley posted photographs and videos of hiking in high heels.Since then, Pattie Gonia has combined outdoor adventures and drag artistry to challenge conventional ideas about who belongs in outdoor spaces.Wiley's activism is closely connected to LGBTQ+ inclusion and community building. Having spoken about the challenges of growing up gay in Nebraska and feeling pressure to conform to traditional expectations of masculinity, Wiley created Pattie Gonia to encourage queer people to express themselves freely and feel welcome in nature. The performer organises outdoor gatherings and group hikes, including events for LGBTQ+ and transgender communities. Wiley also co-founded the Outdoorist Oath in 2022, an initiative focused on environmental protection, inclusion and outdoor exploration, and has supported LGBTQ+ youth through organisations such as Brave Trails.Wiley has raised $3.7 million for environmental causes through performances, social media campaigns and fundraising initiatives. One prominent effort was a 100-mile hike from Point Reyes to San Francisco in December 2025, undertaken in drag to raise money for environmental organisations. The campaign reportedly generated around $1.2 million. Wiley was also named to TIME magazine's 2023 Next Generation Leaders list.Patagonia filed its trademark infringement lawsuit against Wiley and their company, Entrepreneur Enterprises Inc., in the US District Court for the Central District of California on January 21, 2026.The company argues that the name Pattie Gonia is too similar to its own trademark. It alleges that the use of similar logos, designs and branding could lead consumers to believe that the performer or her products are connected to, sponsored by or endorsed by Patagonia.The dispute reportedly dates back to 2022, when Patagonia raised concerns about the name during discussions involving a proposed collaboration with outdoor equipment company Hydro Flask. According to the lawsuit, the parties reached an understanding under which Wiley could continue using the persona for activism and related activities but would not commercialise the name as a brand.Patagonia alleges that Wiley subsequently began selling Pattie Gonia-branded clothing in late 2024 and continued using designs resembling its logos. The company also objected to Wiley's application to trademark the name, filed in 2025. It argues that the branding could weaken the distinctiveness of its trademarks and create confusion about the source of products and services.Despite taking the dispute to federal court, Patagonia is seeking only $1 in nominal monetary damages. Its complaint also asks the court to stop Wiley from using Pattie Gonia as a trademark for apparel and other products, prevent further action on the trademark application and restrict the use of branding it considers too similar to its own.In a statement published in May 2026, Patagonia said it had spent several years trying to find an arrangement that would allow Wiley to continue their activism while protecting its trademarks. The company said the lawsuit was not intended to generate money but to safeguard its intellectual property.Patagonia also said it was not seeking to challenge anyone's identity or right to creative expression, advocacy or protest. Founded in 1973, the company has made environmental activism a central part of its corporate identity and says it has contributed more than $240 million to environmental organisations.Wiley publicly addressed the lawsuit in May 2026, accusing Patagonia of attempting to erase an activist. In an Instagram video and an open letter to the company's leadership, Wiley argued that the case could threaten the identity and community built around the Pattie Gonia persona.Wiley also estimated that the legal fight could cost more than $1 million in legal fees, far exceeding the $1 Patagonia is seeking in damages. They disputed the company's claims about the use of its branding, arguing that some of the examples cited in the lawsuit involved parody and fan art.Wiley has maintained that the name was inspired by Patagonia, the geographical region in South America, rather than being created to imitate the clothing company. They have also said they want to reach an agreement that would allow them to retain the name while respecting Patagonia's intellectual property.The dispute has drawn criticism from supporters and members of the environmental and LGBTQ+ communities. Patagonia, meanwhile, has maintained that it made several attempts to resolve the matter before filing the lawsuit.The disagreement has also moved into a separate proceeding before the US Patent and Trademark Office's Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.On October 2, 2026, Patagonia filed an opposition against Wiley's application to register the PATTIE GONIA trademark. The proceeding was suspended on October 8 pending the outcome of the federal lawsuit, according to the board's official record. The suspension means the trademark application remains contested, but it does not amount to a finding of infringement.The federal case is scheduled for a jury trial on January 26, 2027, with a pretrial conference set for January 11. The court has also referred the parties to private mediation, with a deadline of November 27, 2026.
Article Summary: Pattie Gonia is the stage persona of environmental activist Wyn Wiley. Patagonia is being sued over alleged trademark infringement. Company claims name could create confusion with its established brand. It is seeking just $1 in monetary damages. But it is also seeking restrictions on the use of the name.

Article Title: How TheBurntPeanut turned a small gaming channel into a streaming sensation after making one major change to his content
Article Text:
Image/X

TheBurntPeanut changed his streaming style and found a new identity

How TheBurntPeanut turned funny gaming moments into a growing streaming career

The Streaming world is filled with gamers aspiring to be recognized, but TheBurntPeanut has taken a totally opposite path to get known. Rather than showcasing his real face, he began to appear on screen as a speaking peanut during gaming sessions. This small trick enabled him to establish his identity and attract people through his unique sense of humor and reactions. However, all his fame and recognition did not come about instantly; it took him years before he could discover the right type of content for his viewership.TheBurntPeanut started creating gaming content with a focus on guides and tutorials. He mainly played Escape from Tarkov, a shooting game where players collect items, fight enemies and try to escape safely. However, making guides did not help him attract a large audience. Many other creators were already making similar videos, which made it difficult for him to stand out.His career took a different turn when he decided to change his content in 2024. Instead of continuing with serious gaming guides, he returned to Escape from Tarkov with a funny personality and a virtual peanut avatar. The character became the most recognisable part of his streams.He also started using the game's voice chat to talk to other players. Rather than quietly playing the game, he made jokes, surprised other players and created funny moments during matches. His unusual way of playing a serious shooting game gave viewers something different to enjoy.According to a report by Prima Games in February 2025, this change helped him move from around 200 to 5,000 viewers watching at the same time. His streams also started producing several funny clips that could be shared on social media.Finding a new style was only the beginning. TheBurntPeanut also needed to reach people who had never watched his streams before. He started using platforms like YouTube and TikTok to share short clips from his livestreams. These clips helped more people discover his funny personality without having to watch an entire stream.In 2025, his popularity became even higher. While still playing Escape from Tarkov, he tried some other shooting games too. An important event in his career happened when in October 2025, the game ARC Raiders came out. As he was experienced in such a kind of game, he managed to become one of the popular streamers of this game pretty fast.Also, his streams were supported by collaborations with famous creators like Shroud and Summit1g. According to Streams Charts, he achieved more than 42,000 subscribers watching him streaming Battlefield 6 beta in August 2025.His success also brought recognition from the streaming industry. At The Streamer Awards 2025, he received nominations in three categories: Best FPS Streamer, Best VTuber and Gamer of the Year. He won Best FPS Streamer and Best VTuber.In the end, TheBurntPeanut's story shows how one creative change can make a big difference in a streamer's career.
Article Summary: TheBurntPeanut started creating gaming content with a focus on guides and tutorials. He mainly played Escape from Tarkov, a shooting game where players collect items, fight enemies and try to escape safely. His career took a different turn when he decided to change his content in 2024. He returned to the game with a funny personality and a virtual peanut avatar. The character became the most recognisable part of his streams.

Article Title: 'I wasn't on ballot': Trump shrugs of midterm drubbing, shares photo of what's to come
Article Text:
The defiant response came as Democrats appeared poised to take control of the House of Representatives & Senate

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think contributed most to the Republican losses in the midterms? Voter dissatisfaction with the administration Weak performance by Republican candidates Economic concerns among voters Stronger Democratic campaign efforts 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US President Donald Trump struck a defiant tone after Democrats made major gains in the 2026 US midterm elections. The POTUS claimed that Republicans would have won in a "landslide" had he been on the ballot."I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.During several rallies for Republican candidates, Trump had told voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot and vote.In another post shared minutes later Trump said that he was going to become a political pundit and give reasons on why Republican candidates lost."I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!" he wrote.Continuing his rant, Trump then posted a photo of the MAGA hat embroidered with "VETO", perhaps signalling about what's to come.As a President losing both the Senate and the House severely impacts Trump's plans leaving the POTUS to rely on veto and exective orders to further his agenda.Speaking to Fox News' Peter Doocy, a White House official had earlier said that the mood inside the White House was defiant on Tuesday, arguing that Trump himself was not on the ballot despite repeatedly urging voters in several states to treat the midterm elections as a referendum on his presidency.The official also suggested that Trump's supporters were more likely to turn out when the president was directly on the ballot. Defending the Republican performance, the official said Trump had done a better job promoting several Republican candidates than the candidates had done themselves, pointing to the quality of candidates as another factor in the results."Regardless of how today plays out," the official said, Trump's determination to confront the "Radical Left" would only grow stronger. "Buckle up."The defiant response came as Democrats appeared poised to take control of the House of Representatives, with CNN's Decision Desk projecting a victory for the party. The outcome would give Democrats the power to launch an extensive congressional oversight agenda targeting the Trump administration during the final two years of Trump's term.The results also put Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on course to potentially become the first Black speaker of the House, although he would still need to secure the position through a floor vote when the new Congress convenes.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump struck a defiant tone after Democrats made major gains in the 2026 US midterm elections. The POTUS claimed that Republicans would have won in a "landslide" had he been on the ballot. The defiant response came as Democrats appeared poised to take control of the House of Representatives & Senate.

Article Title: US midterm results: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as first Black woman governor, flips Georgia seat
Article Text:
File photo: Keisha Lance Bottoms

Bottoms focused campaign on economy and policy

Jackson's spending and attacks fail to prevent defeat

Georgia's political landscape faces a new test

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected governor of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman to hold the office after defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson in Tuesday's election, the Associated Press reported.Her victory also marks the first time a Democrat has won the state's gubernatorial race since 1998.A former mayor of Atlanta, Bottoms won despite a significant campaign spending disadvantage, with Jackson having spent more than $200 million of his personal fortune on his campaign. She will succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term.Bottoms' victory also marks a shift in a state where voters have historically been reluctant to elect candidates from Atlanta to the governor's office.According to news agency AP, the growth of Georgia's largest metropolitan area has been reshaping the state's political landscape.Although her election breaks a historic barrier, Bottoms largely focused her campaign on economic issues and her policy proposals rather than the significance of her candidacy.The descendant of enslaved Georgians, she has spoken about her family's history in the state and her grandfather's move from rural Georgia to Atlanta.“I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian,” she said. “I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville.”She also recalled how her grandfather had to “walk through these back doors” of downtown buildings that she would later enter through the front as Atlanta's mayor. She said her ancestry “is always present with me”.On policy, Bottoms called for expanding Medicaid to cover hundreds of thousands more people and raising Georgia's minimum wage to $15 an hour. She also pledged to increase pay for teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees.Her proposals included pausing new data centre developments, stopping the installation of additional automated Flock cameras used by law enforcement, and repealing Georgia's ban on abortions after the sixth week of pregnancy.“This is a life and death issue,” she said of the abortion restrictions, citing cases of women dying from miscarriages and pregnancy complications because doctors feared criminal prosecution under the law.Bottoms also pledged to “make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump”.During the campaign, she repeatedly contrasted her approach with Jackson's stated ambition to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and become the president's “favorite governor”.“I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” Bottoms said during the rivals' only debate. “I’m running to work on behalf of people like you.”Jackson, a businessman who founded Jackson Healthcare, entered the governor's race as a relatively unknown candidate but used his personal wealth and outsider appeal to secure the Republican nomination.He had defeated the sitting lieutenant governor, who had received Trump's early endorsement, as well as the state attorney general and secretary of state.During the general election campaign, Jackson attacked Bottoms' record as Atlanta mayor. His television advertisements featured footage of protests following the 2020 police killings of Rayshard Brooks in Atlanta and George Floyd in Minneapolis. He also criticised Bottoms for not seeking a second term as mayor, accusing her of abandoning the city.Bottoms, in turn, questioned Jackson's claims that he understood the economic difficulties faced by ordinary Georgians. She pointed to his company's government contracts and accused him of using money earned from taxpayers to try to “buy this election”.Bottoms' election comes as Georgia has increasingly become a two-party battleground. Democrats have won three US Senate elections in the state since Trump's first presidential victory a decade ago.The state also re-elected Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff on Tuesday. He will serve alongside Raphael Warnock, Georgia's first Black senator. Ossoff is also the state's first Jewish senator.Bottoms' victory follows three consecutive Georgia gubernatorial elections in which a Black woman led the Democratic ticket. Republican Kemp defeated Stacey Abrams in the previous two contests. Abrams, a prominent voting rights advocate and Democratic fundraiser, did not seek the nomination for a third run.Bottoms was among eight Black major-party nominees for governor on Tuesday's ballot. There have been only three Black governors elected in US history, all Democratic men.This year, Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth of Minnesota were both seeking to become the first Black women elected governor of their respective states.Republicans have controlled Georgia's governorship and both chambers of its General Assembly for more than two decades.Democrats were seeking to flip the state House in Tuesday's elections, while Republicans were expected to retain their Senate majority, leaving Bottoms potentially having to work with at least one Republican-controlled chamber.
Article Summary: Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson. She will succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term. It is the first time a Democrat has won the state's gubernatorial race since 1998. Bottoms largely focused her campaign on economic issues and her policy proposals.

Article Title: In 2016, a Wisconsin man began picking up discarded roadside wood to make art; nine years later, the NFL displayed all 32 team logos he created from scrap furniture after 700 hours of work
Article Text:
From roadside finds to a full-time artistic pursuit

How discarded furniture became 32 NFL logos

A personal connection behind the Buffalo Bills logo

What some people leave behind on roadsides or throw away as unwanted furniture can end up becoming something far more valuable in the hands of the right person. For Ike Wynter, a Wisconsin-based wood artist, discarded wooden objects became the raw material for an unusual artistic journey that eventually took his work to one of America's biggest sporting events. After beginning to collect unwanted wood in 2016, Wynter went on to create all 32 National Football League ( NFL ) team logos using reclaimed furniture, spending hundreds of hours bringing the project to life.According to a report by PEOPLE, Wynter's creations eventually attracted the attention of the NFL, which displayed the collection at the 2025 NFL Draft in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The project reportedly took around 700 hours to complete, turning pieces of unwanted furniture into recognisable symbols of America's professional football teams.Wynter's journey into woodworking started with curiosity and a willingness to see potential in things other people no longer wanted. In 2016, he began picking up discarded pieces of wood from roadsides, curbsides, alleys and dumpsters. Initially, he experimented with turning the material into coffee tables and other household objects before gradually exploring more elaborate forms of art.The Milwaukee native is a self-taught artist who developed his woodworking skills through experience, including working with his father on cutting wood and framing houses.Instead of buying fresh timber for his creations, he began building a collection of reclaimed materials, giving unwanted furniture a second life.His approach also meant that no two pieces of wood were necessarily alike. Old furniture, entertainment centres, wooden pallets and even parts of pianos could become useful material for his work. Rather than covering imperfections with paint, Wynter uses the natural shades, grains and textures of the wood to create different colours and visual details.Over time, his unusual creations began attracting attention online. His videos documenting the process gained millions of views, helping him move from making art as a personal pursuit to receiving commissions and collaborations. Among his notable projects were a wooden podcast logo for former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson and creative collaborations with brands and sporting organisations, including Crayola, the Milwaukee Brewers and Notre Dame.His oversized wooden Crayola crayon box, which went viral in 2024, was another project that brought his work to a wider audience. However, the NFL commission became one of the most demanding assignments of his career.According to the Green Bay Press-Gazette, the NFL approached Wynter towards the end of December 2024 with an unusual proposal. The league wanted him to create wooden mosaics of all 32 NFL team logos for an installation at the 2025 NFL Draft, scheduled to take place at Lambeau Field in Green Bay from April 24 to 26.Each logo measured approximately three feet by three feet. The challenge was not simply reproducing familiar sporting symbols. Wynter had to recreate their colours and intricate details using only the different shades of salvaged wood available to him.He collected more than 50 discarded furniture pieces from across Wisconsin and spent weeks sorting, cutting and matching the materials to the logos. According to his interview with CBS 58, the collection process involved communicating with the NFL's creative team to determine which natural wood tones could work for the different teams. The finished pieces contained no paint or stain. Their colours came entirely from the original wood.The process was far more complicated than working on one logo at a time. A single piece of furniture could provide material for several teams. For instance, wood from one entertainment centre could be used for parts of the Baltimore Ravens, Philadelphia Eagles and New England Patriots logos. Sometimes, however, the artist had to wait weeks before finding the exact shade required to complete a particular section.One particularly interesting discovery came from an old vanity offered by a man on Facebook. The furniture had been gifted to his grandmother in 1934 and was part of a family set. When Wynter removed its mirror, he discovered a weathered wooden sunburst pattern behind it. He immediately recognised its potential and used the material for the rays in the Miami Dolphins logo.The finished collection was installed along the Player Walkway, the passage through which drafted players walked towards the stage after hearing their names announced. The artwork was part of the NFL's broader 2025 Draft theme, 'Built by Community'.NFL Brand Experience Team art director Justin Wright told CBS 58 that Wynter's work stood out because of its distinctive aesthetic and his practice of sourcing materials from the local community. The league saw an opportunity to connect the artist's approach with the event's emphasis on community.While all 32 logos represented an important milestone, one had a particularly personal meaning for Wynter. The Buffalo Bills logo reminded him of his grandfather, Raymond Kuffel, who had been drafted by the team in 1944. Kuffel was later redrafted in 1947 and played professional football between 1947 and 1949. He also attended Marquette University and Notre Dame, where he captained the football team. However, Wynter never got the opportunity to meet him. His grandfather died when his mother was just 16.Speaking to CBS 58, Wynter said creating the Bills logo was the most meaningful part of the project because it gave him an opportunity to feel connected to a family member he had never known.The artist also reserved a special place for his hometown team, the Green Bay Packers. He deliberately saved the team's iconic 'G' for the final part of the collection, making it the last element he completed after spending hundreds of hours on the project.CBS 58 reported that the entire assignment, including sourcing furniture, cutting, assembling, gluing and finishing the pieces, took approximately 600 to 700 hours. Wynter also described working through the night, including three consecutive nights when he remained in his studio until sunrise.The NFL purchased the collection, initially planning to send the pieces to the league's headquarters after the draft, but it was eventually displayed at one of American football's biggest annual events.
Article Summary: Wisconsin-based wood artist Ike Wynter began collecting wood in 2016. He used it to create all 32 National Football League ( NFL ) team logos. The collection was displayed at the 2025 NFL Draft in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The project took around 700 hours to complete. Wynter's grandfather was drafted by the Buffalo Bills in 1944.

Article Title: Fiserv cuts 3,000 employee and contractor jobs since June under its new CEO, including more than 10% of senior management, as the US payments giant doubles its cost-saving target to $1 billion
Article Text:
Pic credit: Reuters

Fiserv has cut its employee and contractor workforce by 3,000 since June, with the reductions reaching deep into the company’s leadership, Reuters reported. Chief Executive Takis Georgakopoulos shared the figures on an earnings call on Tuesday. The same call brought a bigger savings goal, a plan to shed smaller products and a set of numbers that investors had to weigh quickly.Even senior executives were not sparedThe senior management team also took a hit, with a reduction of more than 10% under Georgakopoulos. Fiserv had more than 38,000 employees worldwide as of 31 December 2025, so the latest round affects a significant part of the workforce. The company did not link the cuts to a single division.“We are pursuing a number of initiatives to simplify the organisation and operate more efficiently, including Project Elevate,” Fiserv said in a statement. The programme also underpins the company’s savings target.Project Elevate now aims to save $1 billion, up from $500 million. The change comes after activist investor Jana Partners urged the company to target $1.25 billion in savings. Fiserv has doubled its original goal, although it has stopped short of Jana Partners’ target.The timing of these changes matters.Fiserv reported adjusted earnings of $1.75 per share, slightly ahead of the $1.72 analysts had expected. Revenue fell 1% to $4.85 billion in the third quarter. Management said the company had moved past its weakest revenue period, which was the second quarter.Georgakopoulos also said Fiserv plans to exit more than a dozen smaller products that “lack attractive performance”.In its third-quarter 2026 report, the CEO said: “Our team is executing with urgency, and we are seeing meaningful progress. Net attrition in banking is down more than 25% year to date, major client wins are now ramping, Clover continues to produce consistent underlying growth and our modern merchant platform is gaining momentum. As we simplify and focus our organisation with an AI-everywhere mindset, we have increasing confidence that we can drive greater efficiency while investing in innovation and delivering differentiated client value. ”Meanwhile, shares have risen in pre-market trading following the news, a sign that investors liked the direction. Still, a cost target is a promise, not a result. The company has said Project Elevate will require continued spending before the savings fully show up in its accounts. Fiserv will need to prove that the cuts leave it stronger, not just smaller.
Article Summary: Fiserv has cut its employee and contractor workforce by 3,000 since June. Chief Executive Takis Georgakopoulos shared the figures on an earnings call. Fiserv had more than 38,000 employees worldwide as of 31 December 2025. The company did not link the cuts to a single division.

Article Title: Delaware court orders Faith Evans to pay $12.5 million to Notorious B.I.G.'s mother's trust in estate dispute after widow challenges its claim to millions in music business distributions
Article Text:
Why Notorious B.I.G.'s estate is at the centre of a $12.5 million legal battle

Why Faith Evans challenged the trust's claim to millions

Who is Wayne Barrow and how did he enter the dispute?

Biggie's son C.J. is involved in a separate legal battle

What happens to the $12.5 million and the interest?

A Delaware court has ordered singer Faith Evans to ensure a payment of $12,518,336 from Notorious B.I.G. LLC to a trust established by the late rapper's mother, Voletta Wallace, following a legal dispute over millions generated by his music business. The October 27 ruling by the Delaware Court of Chancery also awards prejudgment interest on the distributions, calculated from the dates the payments were made and compounded quarterly. The case centres on the financial rights attached to Wallace's ownership interest in the company after her death in February 2025. Evans, who manages the company, had challenged the trust's entitlement to distributions made before it formally became a member, arguing that it was owed only $48,612.The disagreement over the trust's entitlement to these distributions eventually became the central issue in the $12.5 million legal battle. While Evans maintained that the trust could claim only the money distributed after it formally became a member of the company, Voletta's estate argued that her financial rights had passed to the trust immediately after her death. The Delaware court ultimately sided with the trust, ruling that it was entitled to distributions dating back to February 2025.The disagreement centred on the difference between becoming a formal member of a limited liability company and inheriting the financial rights attached to an existing ownership interest.The trust formally became a member of Notorious B.I.G. LLC on December 12, 2025, after executing the required instrument under the company's operating agreement. Evans and the company argued that the trust should therefore receive only $48,612, representing distributions attributable to its 25% share after that date.However, the company had made several substantial distributions following Wallace's death. These included payments of $4 million each on March 20, June 30 and September 25, 2025, followed by another $469,724 on December 26.Evans and the company argued that the earlier amounts should not be released while a separate legal challenge involving Wayne Barrow, the trustee of Voletta's estate, remained unresolved in Pennsylvania.The court rejected that position, distinguishing between the trust's formal membership status and its economic rights. It ruled that Wallace's financial interest in the company transferred to her estate immediately upon her death and subsequently passed to the trust under her will. As a result, the trust was entitled to distributions dating back to February 21, 2025, even though its formal membership began months later.Wayne Barrow, the late rapper's former manager, initiated the Delaware lawsuit in July 2025 on behalf of Voletta Wallace's trust.Wallace had appointed Barrow as the sole trustee of her revocable trust and executor of her estate shortly before her death. He subsequently sought to exercise the trust's rights in Notorious B.I.G. LLC, including its entitlement to distributions and recognition of its ownership interest.Barrow alleged that Evans had prevented him from exercising those rights and recognising the trust's position within the company.In August 2026, Delaware Chancellor Kathaleen St. J. McCormick granted Barrow's motion for summary judgment on two claims and dismissed the defendants' counterclaim. The October 27 decision subsequently addressed the outstanding questions concerning the trust's membership date and its entitlement to earlier distributions.The judge also noted that Barrow had received Letters Testamentary on April 21, 2025, establishing his authority as the estate's executor.The dispute over the rapper's estate has also drawn in his son, Christopher Jordan Wallace, known as C.J., who is challenging Barrow's appointment in a separate Pennsylvania proceeding.Voletta Wallace had initially named her grandson as a successor trustee. However, shortly before her death, she amended her estate arrangements, removing him from that position and appointing Barrow as the sole trustee instead.C.J. subsequently challenged the changes, questioning the circumstances surrounding his grandmother's decision to appoint Barrow and his authority over the estate.Evans and the company relied on this separate dispute while arguing that the money should not be released to the trust until the Pennsylvania proceedings were resolved.However, the Delaware court ruled that the pending challenge would not affect the economic rights already transferred to the trust. It also found that Barrow's actions as executor, supported by his Letters Testamentary, did not need to be suspended pending the outcome of the separate case.In its October 27 decision, the Delaware Court of Chancery determined that the Voletta Wallace Revocable Trust was entitled to $12,518,336 in distributions made after Wallace's death.The court also awarded prejudgment interest on the amount, calculated from the dates on which the individual distributions were made. The interest is to be charged at Delaware's statutory rate and compounded quarterly.The judge instructed Barrow to submit a final proposed order within 20 days, incorporating the October decision and the court's earlier rulings.According to a statement shared with PEOPLE, Barrow's lawyer said Evans was ordered to have Notorious B.I.G. LLC pay the trust more than $14 million, including interest, by November 10. He also said he hoped she would comply with the order.Voletta Wallace's estate arrangements direct assets not specifically bequeathed elsewhere towards the Christopher Wallace Memorial Foundation, established in memory of her son. The foundation supports young people through educational opportunities and mentorship initiatives.
Article Summary: A Delaware court has ordered singer Faith Evans to ensure a payment of $12,518,336 from Notorious B.I.G. LLC to a trust established by the late rapper's mother, Voletta Wallace. The case centres on the financial rights attached to Wallace's ownership interest in the company after her death in February 2025. Evans, who manages the company, had challenged the trust's entitlement to distributions made before it formally became a member.

Article Title: In 2024, Floyd Mayweather rented a Manhattan apartment for $100,000 a month; two years later, a court reportedly ordered him to pay about $340,000 in a rent dispute while the owners sold it for $20 mi
Article Text:
The Centners combined two adjoining apartments, purchased for over $15 million, into a five-bedroom Manhattan duplex.

A $100,000-a-month Manhattan home

When the rent stopped coming

The apartment finds a buyer for $20 million

A costly end to the dispute

A luxury address with a $100,000 monthly price tag

From lawsuit to unpaid rent

Controversial $20 million sale

Last verdict

Floyd Mayweather Jr. may have spent his boxing career making sure he never lost a fight, but a rental dispute in Manhattan has given the retired champion an entirely different kind of battle. A luxury apartment he once called home, and for which he agreed to pay $100,000 a month, is now at the centre of a court judgment ordering him to pay nearly $340,000 in outstanding dues. Interestingly, while the legal tussle was unfolding, the property's owners managed to sell the residence for a reported $20 million.Mayweather's association with the property began in December 2024, when he rented a lavish duplex at The Baccarat Hotel and Residences in Manhattan.According to The Real Deal, the residence is located at 20 West 53rd Street and occupies space across the building's 18th and 19th floors.The apartment belonged to Miami-based entrepreneurs Leila and David Centner, who had bought two adjoining units for more than $15 million and combined them into a five-bedroom, five-bathroom home. At $100,000 a month, the rental was hardly an ordinary residential arrangement, even by Manhattan's luxury property standards.But the expensive address soon became the setting for a disagreement over money.According to Realtor, Mayweather allegedly stopped paying rent midway through 2025, prompting the Centners to take legal action through an LLC. The owners initially sought around $500,000 in unpaid rent and damages, before both sides worked out a settlement.Under the agreement, Mayweather was expected to clear his outstanding dues by December 2, 2025. The Real Deal claims he paid for a month before going dark again. According to the owners, he did not answer their calls or respond to the court complaint.The situation became particularly frustrating for the owners when Mayweather continued sharing glimpses of his lavish lifestyle online. Realtor and The Real Deal report that an Instagram post showing stacks of cash caught the Centners' attention while they were still trying to recover their money.With Mayweather no longer occupying the residence, the owners decided to put it back on the rental market. Rena Kliot of Pulse International Realty was involved in relisting the apartment at $150,000 a month.The property, however, eventually found a buyer. According to The Real Deal, the Centners sold the duplex for $20 million last week, with the transaction appearing in property records. The sale marked a substantial exit for the owners, who had originally invested more than $15 million in the two units.The rental disagreement has now reached another milestone. A New York state court judge issued a default judgment against Mayweather, ordering him to pay approximately $340,000. As reported by Realtor and The Real Deal, the amount includes outstanding rent, late fees, interest, legal expenses and other associated costs.The development adds to a series of legal matters involving the former boxer. The Real Deal also reported that Mayweather dropped a lawsuit in September against his former investment manager, Jona Rechnitz, whom he had accused of misappropriating $175 million.For the Centners, the Manhattan apartment has already changed hands for $20 million. The rent dispute, meanwhile, has left Mayweather with a court-ordered bill that is considerably more expensive than a month's stay at the luxury address.According to The Real Deal, Mayweather began renting a sprawling duplex at The Baccarat Hotel and Residences in December 2024, agreeing to pay $100,000 every month. Located at 20 West 53rd Street, the residence formed part of two adjoining apartments on the building's 18th and 19th floors.The property belonged to Miami-based entrepreneurs Leila and David Centner, who had purchased the two units for more than $15 million before combining them into an expansive five-bedroom, five-bathroom residence. The former boxer was lavishly hosted at the Baccarat development, known for its luxury hospitality and housing.However, what began as an exclusive rental arrangement eventually developed into a financial disagreement between the tenant and the owners.A real estate agent said Mayweather stopped paying rent monthly in mid-2025, starting the fight. The owners sued through a limited liability company for unpaid rent and other damages.The Real Deal puts the initial amount owed at approximately $500,000, including unpaid rent and other associated costs. The two sides eventually negotiated a settlement under which Mayweather was expected to clear his outstanding dues by December 2, 2025.However, the settlement did not satisfy the property owners. The Real Deal reported that Mayweather paid one month's debt but stopped communicating. The owners also alleged that repeated attempts to contact him went unanswered.Mayweather's social media posts reportedly frustrated the Centners. “The owners were particularly upset when they discovered an Instagram post featuring stacks of money, even though they failed to collect rent arrears,” the realtor said.With the rental arrangement behind them, the owners turned their attention to selling the property. Rena Kliot of Pulse International Realty, who was involved in relisting the residence for $150,000 per month after Mayweather's departure, worked with the sellers on the transaction.According to The Real Deal, the duplex was eventually sold for $20 million last week, with property records confirming the transaction.After Mayweather allegedly failed to respond to the lawsuit or appear in court, a New York state court default judgment was issued. The ruling directs him to pay approximately $340,000, covering unpaid rent, late fees, interest, legal fees and related expenses, as reported by Realtor and The Real Deal.The judgment marks another chapter in the former champion's legal affairs. In September, The Real Deal reported that Mayweather had dropped a lawsuit against his former investment manager, Jona Rechnitz, whom he had accused of diverting $175 million.While the Manhattan property has now found a new owner, the financial dispute surrounding Mayweather's former luxury address has left an expensive reminder of a rental arrangement that went considerably off course.Images Courtesy: Instgram/onlyfullflights and istock
Article Summary: Floyd Mayweather Jr. agreed to pay $100,000 a month for a five-bedroom duplex at The Baccarat Hotel and Residences in Manhattan in December 2024. The property belonged to Miami-based entrepreneurs Leila and David Centner, who had bought two adjoining units for more than $15 million. Mayweather allegedly stopped paying rent midway through 2025, prompting the Centners to take legal action through an LLC. The owners initially sought around $500,000 in unpaid rent and damages, before both sides worked out a settlement. Mayweather was expected to clear his outstanding dues by December 2, 2025.

Article Title: In 1992, a trucker paid $5 for a drip painting at a San Bernardino thrift shop; a fingerprint said Pollock, experts said no, and she died in 2019 refusing $50 million
Article Text:
Photograph of Jackson Pollock. Image credits: Wikipedia

A $5 thrift shop purchase led to an unexpected discovery

A fingerprint examination pointed towards Pollock’s studio

Art specialists rejected the Pollock attribution

The studio floor at the Pollock-Kransner House in Springs, New York. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Horton declined millions, but never sold the painting

Who the $&% Is Jackson Pollock?

An oil painting purchased at a thrift store in California for $5 dollars, sparked a legal battle over its provenance as a work by the most famous American abstract painter. Teri Horton, a truck driver from California, purchased the painting to give it as a present to a friend. At the time, she had no idea that the artwork might be an original painting by Jackson Pollock, whose works have sold for millions of dollars. The story started in 1992; however, arguments about the painting’s origins have gone on far beyond that year. Although forensic art expert Paul Biro claimed that a fingerprint on the painting matched one found on a paint can in Pollock’s former studio, the evidence did not establish that Pollock had created the artwork.According to the Los Angeles Times, Horton bought the 66-by-48-inch painting for $5 at Dot’s Thrift Shop in San Bernardino, California, in 1992. Her plan was to give the canvas to her friend. However, it was too big to pass through the entrance of her friend's trailer. Later on, she decided to sell the canvas at a yard sale. Upon observing the canvas, an art teacher proposed that the artwork could be one of Pollock’s works.Initially, Horton was unaware of Pollock as an artist. Nevertheless, the suggestion urged her to find out more about it. He became popular by using drips, pours and splashes of paint on huge canvases. It seemed reasonable due to Pollock's style. However, the only thing visual similarities could not prove was the painter.Eventually, Horton contacted forensic art expert Paul Biro from Canada. During his examination, Biro reported finding a partial fingerprint in paint on the back of the canvas. According to CNN’s 2007 report, Biro compared the fingerprint found on the back of Horton’s canvas with one he identified on a paint can in Pollock’s former studio in East Hampton, New York. Biro claimed that the partial fingerprints on the canvas matched a print on a paint can from Pollock’s former East Hampton studio. He argued that the match connected the painting to the artist’s studio, although he did not independently establish Pollock as its creator. André Turcotte, a retired fingerprint examiner with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, supported Biro’s fingerprint comparison.However, apart from studying the prints, Biro analysed the paintings, material composition and condition as well. According to his conclusion, the painting had enough similarities to be made by Pollock, but this conclusion didn’t confirm the artist's authenticity without doubt. After consulting a team of Pollock specialists, IFAR concluded that the painting was not by Jackson Pollock. According to CBS News, IFAR’s expert acknowledged that the painting had some strong similarities to authentic Pollock works, but concluded that it was not by his hand.IFAR tested the painting and sought the views of experts acquainted with Pollock’s style of painting. After consulting a team of Pollock’s specialists, there were issues related to provenance that added more complications to the case.The painting had no signature and had no ownership history linking it to Pollock. By the time Horton started investigating the painting's origin, Dot’s Thrift Shop had been torn down and its owner had died. It was hard for anyone to trace the origins of the painting or know how it came into the hands of the owners of the thrift shop.Nevertheless, Horton was sure that the canvas was authentic. There is a difference in the reports about the potential buyers’ offers; CBS reported that there was at least one art collector willing to pay $2 million, while the Los Angeles Times mentioned the art dealers as the source of the offer. Horton also reportedly rejected a $9 million offer from a Saudi collector, according to The New Yorker. In a 2007 interview with CBS News, Horton said she believed the painting was worth at least $50 million, although no independent valuation or confirmed offer of that amount was established. This amount referred to the price, which she expected from the sale of the canvas. The story became well known through the documentary filmThat described her attempts to prove the authenticity of the work. Horton passed away on July 8, 2019, being 86 years old. At the time of her death, the artist of the canvas was not established. It remained disputable and unauthenticated and there was no conclusion about the artist who created it.
Article Summary: An oil painting purchased at a thrift store in California for $5 dollars, sparked a legal battle over its provenance as a work by the most famous American abstract painter. Teri Horton, a truck driver from California, purchased the painting to give it as a present to a friend. At the time, she had no idea that the artwork might be an original painting by Jackson Pollock. Forensic art expert Paul Biro claimed that a fingerprint on the painting matched one found on a paint can in Pollock’s former studio. But the evidence did not establish that Pollock had created the artwork.

Article Title: The family of soul legend Otis Redding opened an $11.2 million arts centre in his hometown; the facility gives young musicians recording studios and songwriting spaces
Article Text:
Image Credit: Greater Macon Chamber of Commerce

The Otis Redding arts centre is helping young musicians

A permanent home for the Redding Foundation's music programmes

What can students learn inside the centre

The centre reaches more than 1,000 students in its first year

A musical legacy rooted in Macon's history

The family of soul music legend Otis Redding has opened an $11.2 million arts centre in his hometown of Macon, Georgia, offering young people access to recording studios, songwriting rooms and musical instruments. The facility, established by the Otis Redding Foundation, provides a permanent home for the family's longstanding efforts to introduce children to music and creative expression. Opened in March 2025, the centre brings together education, performance and technology under one roof, continuing the singer's legacy while giving a new generation opportunities to explore its musical ambitions.According to the Macon Telegraph's report, the Otis Redding Center for the Arts covers approximately 15,000 square feet in downtown Macon.Its modern design incorporates 7 creative labs, private lesson rooms, practice spaces, a songwriting lounge and a professional recording studio.The building also includes an indoor-outdoor amphitheatre, providing space for performances and gatherings. Students can move between different areas depending on whether they want to practice an instrument, collaborate with other musicians or develop their own compositions.The centre was created to support children and teenagers aged 5 to 18, accommodating beginners as well as those with more advanced musical experience. Its facilities include approximately 250 instruments, among them pianos, trumpets, violins, trombones, drums and other percussion equipment.The building also incorporates vintage musical memorabilia and vinyl records, connecting students with the artists and musical traditions that came before them.The centre represents an important development for the Otis Redding Foundation, which had been running music camps and educational programmes without a permanent physical facility of its own.As Georgia Public Broadcasting reported, the foundation had spent years teaching young musicians and songwriters through summer camps and after-school activities. The new building brought those initiatives together in a dedicated environment designed for learning, creativity and performance.The foundation's family members have continued to develop the singer's legacy through education and community programmes. The arts centre gives those efforts a permanent base in the city where Redding's musical journey began.The facility was also made possible through substantial community support. The Macon Melody reported that Zelma Redding, Otis Redding's widow, donated the land for the project, while the foundation raised more than $11 million to construct the building.The opening ceremony took place on March 18, 2025, with community members, local officials and the Redding family gathering at the Zelma Redding Amphitheater to celebrate the completion of the project.The facility is intended to provide more than conventional music lessons. Students can explore songwriting, instrument playing, recording, audio mixing and the technical aspects of producing music.According to the Macon Telegraph, experienced musicians and industry professionals are expected to teach students how to play instruments, create sheet music, write lyrics and record audio. The centre also offers opportunities for students to work together, experiment with sounds and develop their own musical ideas.One of its most distinctive features is the O3 Recording Studio, named in memory of Otis Redding III, the singer's son who died in 2023. The studio was designed by engineer Neils Kastor, whose previous work includes recording facilities associated with Katy Perry, P!nk and Dr Dre.The studio incorporates carefully designed acoustic features, including stone walls, a raised concrete floor and specially arranged wooden elements to help produce clear sound. Students can use the professional recording environment to turn their musical ideas into finished recordings.There is a songwriting lounge and soundproof listening spaces, which allow young people to work independently or collaborate without distractions.The arts centre's early impact has been reflected in the number of young people who have already benefited from its programmes.In an April 7, 2026 report, the Macon Chamber of Commerce said the centre had served more than 1,000 students through its programmes and school visits during its first year.Karla Redding-Andrews, Otis Redding's daughter, described the progress as particularly meaningful because the facility was created to ensure children could experience the opportunities offered by music and the arts.The centre has also developed into a gathering place for young musicians from across Georgia.Otis Redding remains one of the most influential figures in soul music. Born in Georgia, the singer became internationally recognised for his powerful voice and songs, including Respect and (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay. He died in a plane crash in December 1967, aged 26.His family's continued investment in music education reflects the importance of giving young people opportunities that he valued during his lifetime.The centre's location also carries personal significance. The facility stands close to places associated with Redding's history in downtown Macon, placing the educational project within the city's wider musical heritage.The building's design deliberately combines contemporary technology with traditional musical experiences. Vinyl records, acoustic instruments and memorabilia sit alongside digital recording equipment and modern creative laboratories, helping students understand both the history and future of music.
Article Summary: The Otis Redding Center for the Arts opened in Macon, Georgia, in March 2025. The facility is a permanent home for the Redding Foundation's music programmes. It offers young people access to recording studios, songwriting rooms and instruments. The centre is intended to support children and teenagers aged 5 to 18.

Article Title: In 1990, Oregon trucked 580,000 tyres up to 200 miles to shore up slide-prone US 42; net cost $10 a ton, and federal engineers called it the largest tyre fill for a landslide correction project
Article Text:
AI Representation: Oregon used 580,000 discarded tyres to stabilise a landslide-prone US Route. Image credits: Chatgpt

Highway construction reactivated an existing landslide

Four suppliers delivered 580,000 shredded tyres

Oregon recycling program reduced the material cost to $10 per

Shredded tyre materials. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

FHWA identified it as the largest known landslide-correction project

Discarded car tyres usually create a waste management problem, but Oregon engineers found an unusual use for thousands of them during a highway repair project in 1990. A slope along a road embankment was unstable and adding more regular soil would have put more weight on ground that was already moving. Instead, the Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT) replaced part of the heavy soil embankment with shredded scrap tyres, a lighter material that cut the load on the unstable slope. The work took place in 1990 on US 42, the Coos Bay-Roseburg Highway, about 25 miles west of Roseburg in southwestern Oregon. ODOT’s report lists the route as Oregon state route 35. The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) later cited it as the largest known use of shredded tyres in a landslide correction project.The project was carried out in 1990 on US Highway 42, also known as ODOT Highway 35 along the Coos Bay-Roseburg route about 25 miles west of Roseburg in southwestern Oregon, which is referred to as Oregon State Road 35 in the ODOT engineering report. Modification of the embankment through Highway upgrading led to the reactivation of an old landslide underneath the road due to the increased load.The need for a repair measure that could stabilise the slope without increasing its load required a design whereby part of the soil embankment was replaced by shredded chips. The soil from excavation was used to create a counterweight at the bottom of the slope. ODOT documented the work in its February 1991 report, Experimental Project: Use of Shredded Tires for Lightweight Fill. The job needed about 5,800 tons of shredded tyres, roughly 580,000 tyres. Four suppliers trucked them to the site from 150 to 275 miles away, according to the 1993 paper by Richard J. Upton and George Machan in Transportation Research Record 1422. The chips arrived in 100-cubic-yard trucks, each carrying 28 tons. Workers placed them in three-foot lifts and compacted each lift with a D-8 dozer. Handling the material caused some trouble. Exposed steel wire in the shreds punctured some of the dump-truck tyres used on the job. The 1993 paper by Upton and Machan covers the supply and construction in more detail.Oregon’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) backed the project through a program that reimbursed the productive use of scrap tyres. The shredded material cost $30 per ton and DEQ refunded $20, bringing the material cost down to $10 per ton. Placing and compacting it added $8.33 per ton, for an installed cost of $18.33 per ton. The reimbursement made shredded tyres a practical option for the repair.After construction, the tyre fill got a three-foot compacted soil cap on the top and side slopes. The road surface went on top: 23 inches of aggregate base under 8 inches of asphalt pavement. The thickest part of the tyre embankment was about 12.5 feet. Under the weight of the cover, it settled about 20 inches, roughly 13 percent of its original thickness.ODOT monitored the structure with slope inclinometers, piezometers, settlement plates and survey hubs. The 1993 study found that the pavement’s initial deflection was about double the deflection over an earth embankment.The project appeared in the FHWA’s User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction. The guidelines called Oregon’s use of about 580,000 scrap tyres the largest known use of shredded tyres in a landslide correction project. That record covers landslide repairs only, not every highway embankment that used recycled tyres. The FHWA also set up another project in Colorado where about 400,000 to 450,000 tyres were used in an interstate Highway embankment. The repair conducted in Oregon showed that old tyres could be used as a lightweight material for construction purposes, especially when normal soil puts pressure on the unstable land.
Article Summary: Oregon used 580,000 discarded tyres to stabilise a landslide-prone US Route. The Federal Highway Administration said it was the largest known use of shredded tyres in a landslide correction project. The shredded material cost $30 per ton and DEQ refunded $20, bringing the material cost down to $10 per ton.

Article Title: A Washington man was due to inherit his father's ranch, but a court found he had financially abused his father and the land went to his children; 14 years later, an appeals court upheld $166,698.50 in
Article Text:
Representative image

The ranch and the divorce

The inheritance falls apart

Representative image of abuse

Evans tries to undo the judgments

The 2021 extension and the line

Why the appeal failed

What the ruling means

Calvin Evans Jr. expected to inherit his father’s Washington ranch, a property that had also become central to his divorce from Deborah Evans, now Deborah Bunney. During the couple’s 2011 dissolution, a court awarded Bunney the full $174,000 the marital community had invested in improvements to the ranch, based on the expectation that Evans would receive the property from his father. But a separate probate dispute later found that Evans had financially abused his father, leaving him with nothing from the estate and sending the ranch to Evans’s four adult children. Fourteen years after the divorce judgments were entered, Evans asked a court to undo them because the anticipated inheritance never arrived. On November 2, 2026, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, refused. It upheld two divorce judgments totalling $166,698.50 against Evans, along with a 2021 order extending them, concluding that his challenge came too late and that the loss of the inheritance was not an extraordinary circumstance justifying relief, as per Justia U.S. Law. Read more details about it here:Evans and Bunney lived and worked on the ranch owned by Evans’s father during the later years of their marriage. The marital community invested at least $174,000 in improvements to the property. Evans’s father’s 2006 will left the ranch to Evans, and that expected inheritance became a major factor in the couple’s divorce.The dissolution court entered its decree on September 15, 2011. Because it found Evans would retain more than $800,000 in ranch property, it awarded Bunney the entire $174,000 community investment. The decree included two monetary judgments against Evans, one for $162,190.50 and another for $4,508, bringing the principal total to $166,698.50.The decree treated the ranch as Evans’s property only if he inherited it from his father, subject to Bunney’s $174,000 lien. It also said the court retained jurisdiction to reconsider the financial distribution if Evans did not succeed under his father’s will but received property through intestate succession or another route.While the divorce was still pending, Evans’s three siblings filed a petition under Washington’s Trust and Estate Disputed Resolution Act, known as TEDRA. They sought to invalidate the will on grounds including lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence, and asked the court to declare Evans an abuser under the applicable statute, which would prevent him from inheriting his father’s property.On May 31, 2012, the TEDRA court found that Evans had financially abused his father. As a result, Evans received nothing from his father’s estate, and the ranch passed to Evans’s four adult children. The Washington Court of Appeals later affirmed that decision in 2015.The property did not disappear from Evans’s financial life entirely. Two of his children, Cory and Jesse Evans, later transferred their combined 50 percent interest in the ranch to Hidden River Ranch LLC, a company Evans solely owned, in exchange for his agreement to leave each child 50 percent of any ranch interest he held. That arrangement meant that, although Evans did not inherit the land directly, his company acquired half of it through his children.After losing the TEDRA appeal, Evans moved in May 2017 to vacate the two 2011 divorce judgments and redistribute the couple’s property. The dissolution court denied the motion without prejudice, saying it needed more information about the outcome of Bunney’s separate unjust-enrichment lawsuit against the estate and those who ultimately inherited the ranch.That separate lawsuit ultimately failed. In March 2019, the court dismissed Bunney’s unjust-enrichment claims with prejudice. By then, the dissolution court had also denied Bunney’s request to place a lien on the ranch because Hidden River Ranch was not a party to the divorce case, while noting that it had previously declined to vacate the divorce judgment and maintained that position.Despite that clear signal, Evans did not renew his request to vacate the judgments. The appeals court later found that he had the information he needed by March 2019, but waited until April 2025 to file another motion for relief.In July 2021, Bunney applied to extend the 2011 judgments for another 10 years under Washington’s judgment-enforcement statute. The dissolution court granted the extension on July 16, 2021, allowing execution on the judgments during the additional period.The ranch was later ordered sold in a partition action because it could not be divided effectively. In December 2024, the partition court found that Bunney was the judgment creditor, that the principal amount of the judgments was $166,698.50, that Evans had made no payments, and that interest was accruing at 12 percent per year. The court then granted Bunney a charging lien against any portion of the sale proceeds to which Evans or his interest in Hidden River Ranch was entitled.Evans said he only learned of the 2021 extension in December 2024, when Bunney sought that lien. About five months later, in April 2025, he moved to vacate both the original judgments and the extension order.The appeals court reviewed the trial court’s refusal to vacate the judgments for abuse of discretion. It concluded there was none. Evans’s challenge to the original 2011 judgments was untimely because he knew by 2012 that he had not inherited the ranch, and he had the information needed to renew his motion by March 2019.The court also rejected Evans’s argument that Bunney’s failure to give notice of the 2021 extension required vacating it. Under the statute, an extension is granted as a matter of right, and the limited issues a court may consider are timeliness, partial satisfaction and calculation errors.
